Boundedness in a fully parabolic chemotaxis system with nonlinear diffusion and sensitivity, and logistic source

Abstract.

In this paper we study the zero-flux chemotaxis-system

{ut=∇⋅((u+1)m−1∇u−(u+1)αχ(v)∇v)+ku−μu2x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v​ux∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot((u+1)^{m-1}\nabla u-(u+1)^{\alpha}\chi(v)\nabla v)+ku-\mu u^{2}&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-vu&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \end{cases}

Ω\Omega being a bounded and smooth domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, and where m,k∈ℝm,k\in\mathbb{R}, μ>0\mu>0 and α<m+12\alpha<\frac{m+1}{2}. For any v≥0v\geq 0 the chemotactic sensitivity function is assumed to behave as the prototype χ⁡(v)=χ0(1+a​v)2\chi(v)=\frac{\chi_{0}}{(1+av)^{2}}, with a≥0a\geq 0 and χ0>0\chi_{0}>0. We prove that for nonnegative and sufficiently regular initial data u⁡(x,0)u(x,0) and v⁡(x,0),v(x,0), the corresponding initial-boundary value problem admits a global bounded classical solution provided μ\mu is large enough.

Key words and phrases: 
Nonlinear parabolic systems, chemotaxis, logistic source, global existence, boundedness.

1. Introduction and motivations

The expression chemotaxis indicates the movement of cells occupying a space, which are stimulated by a chemical signal produced by a substance therein inhomogeneously distributed. Different studies and experiments on bacteria show how they direct their natural motion and change randomly their course precisely depending on the intensity of the chemical gradient stimulus.

In 1971, Keller and Segel (see [9]) proposed a model for the description of the traveling band behavior of bacteria due to the chemotactic response; its mathematical formulation defined in an interval I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} reads:

(1) {ut=ux​x−χ​(u​v−1​vx)xx∈I,t>0,vt=ε​vx​x−u​f​(v)x∈I,t>0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=u_{xx}-\chi(uv^{-1}v_{x})_{x}&x\in I,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\varepsilon v_{xx}-uf(v)&x\in I,t>0.\end{array}\right.

In this model, the distribution of the cells and the concentration of the chemical signal in a point xx of II and at an instant tt of time are, respectively, identified with the functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t). In addition, ε>0\varepsilon>0 represents the diffusion coefficient of the chemical substance, χ\chi is called chemosensitivity and essentially measures the drift velocity of the bacteria through the direction of the gradient of concentration of the chemoattractant and f⁡(v)f(v) denotes a kinetic function describing the chemical reaction between bacteria and the chemical. In terms of the value of the constant ε\varepsilon and the expression of the function ff, some results concerning the existence of traveling wave solutions to system (1) have been established, under proper boundary and initial conditions. For instance, the same [9] corresponds to the limit case ε=0\varepsilon=0 and f⁡(v)=α>0f(v)=\alpha>0, [18] to ε>0\varepsilon>0 and f⁡(v)=α>0f(v)=\alpha>0 and [13] to ε>0\varepsilon>0 and f⁡(v)=α​v>0f(v)=\alpha v>0, with α>0.\alpha>0.

A possible extension to higher dimensions of (1) is described by this initial-boundary value problem

(2) {ut=Δu−χ∇(u⋅∇v)x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−u​vx∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0​and​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla(u\cdot\nabla v)&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0\,\,\textrm{and}\,\,\,v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where χ>0\chi>0, Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, with n≥2n\geq 2, is a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and u0​(x)=u​(x,0)u_{0}(x)=u(x,0) and v0​(x)=v​(x,0)v_{0}(x)=v(x,0) are the initial cells distribution and chemical concentration. Moreover, since ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} indicates the outward normal derivative on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, with zero-flux boundary conditions on both uu and vv, (2) describes the dynamic of a cells population in response to a chemical substance which mutually interact in a totally insulated domain.

Let us observe that for positive cells and chemical distributions, the term −u​v-uv in the second equation of (2) shows that in such a model the signal is progressively consumed by cells; this, naturally, suggests that vv remains bounded through the time. This situation is far to be similar in the classical Keller-Segel model (see [8]), where −u​v-uv reads −v+u-v+u and, hence, the corresponding formulation

(3) {ut=Δu−χ∇(u⋅∇v)x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+ux∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0​and​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla(u\cdot\nabla v)&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0\,\,\textrm{and}\,\,\,v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

manifests how an increasing of the cells favors a production of the signal, so that no bound for vv is a priori expected. Thereafter, even though they are deeply connected, the two models (2) and (3) present different properties. In particular, for system (3), which has been widely discussed from many authors, it is known that in a one-dimensional domain its solutions are global and uniformly bounded in time (see [19]), while in the nn-dimensional context, with n≥2n\geq 2, unbounded solutions idealizing the so called chemotactic collapse (an uncontrolled gathering of cells in proximity of some zones of the space occurring in a certain blow-up time) have been detected e.g. in [6] and [33]. In accordance with this, estimates from below for the blow-up time of unbounded solutions to (3) are explicitly derived in [20].

Now, in order to better contextualize this present investigation in the frame of the existent literature, we precise that an analysis of the previous last contributions highlights as, in higher dimensions (n≥2n\geq 2) and under suitable smallness assumptions on the initial data u0u_{0} and v0v_{0}, the solution to model (3) is global and bounded while there exist blow-up solutions to model (3) for large initial data u0u_{0}. On the opposite side, it has been shown that the global existence or blow-up of solutions to model (2) is independent of the initial data u0u_{0}. Specifically, Tao (see [21]) proves that, for sufficiently regular u0u_{0} and v0v_{0}, if

(4) 0<χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)≤16​(n+1),0<\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{1}{6(n+1)},

then the corresponding initial-boundary value problem (2) possesses a unique global solution that is uniformly bounded, remaining indeed still open the question whether there exist blow-up solutions to the same system for large initial data v0v_{0} or large chemotactic parameter χ\chi not complying with (4). Moreover, continuing on the state of the art of the chemotaxis-consumption model (2), for the three-dimensional setting, in [23] weak solutions that become smooth after some time are constructed. Further, by interpreting the same system as the special case of the general coupled chemotaxis-fluid model, proposed by Goldstein in [24], where exactly the fluid does not give any direct contribution, in [32] the existence of global classical and weak solutions for n=2n=2 and n=3n=3, respectively, is discussed while [34] deals with the stabilization properties of these two-dimensional solutions (we also cite [35] and [36] for existence results to systems close to the same (2) but involving matrix-valued sensitivities).

Exactly in order to contrast undesired blow-up singularities, which as mentioned above may emerge in both models (2) and (3), more complete formulations to these systems with nontrivial sources have been considered; precisely, a complementation of these models through largely used logistic-type effects seems totally natural (see also [15] and [25] for another expression for the source). For instance, for the system

(5) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+g(u)x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+ux∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+g(u)&x\,\in\,\Omega,\,\,\,t>0,\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u&x\,\in\,\Omega,\,\,\,t>0,\end{cases}

defined in a convex smooth and bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1 and endowed with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, in [11] the existence of global weak solutions for χ=τ=1\chi=\tau=1 and g⁡(u)=k​u−μ​u2g(u)=ku-\mu u^{2}, for k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R} and μ\mu positive constant (the classical logistic source), is established for any nonnegative and sufficient regular initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) and arbitrarily small values of μ>0\mu>0; moreover, if n=3n=3, these solutions become classical after some time and provided that kk is not too large. On the other hand, under the same assumptions on the domain and the boundary conditions, for a source gg generalizing the logistic source and verifying g⁡(0)≥0g(0)\geq 0 and g⁡(s)≤k−μ​s2g(s)\leq k-\mu s^{2}, for s≥0s\geq 0, k≥0k\geq 0 and μ,τ\mu,\tau positive and χ∈ℝ\chi\in\mathbb{R}, in [30] the author proves that if μ\mu is big enough, for all sufficiently smooth and nonnegative initial data u0u_{0} and v0v_{0}, system (5) possesses a unique bounded and global-in-time classical solution. Additionally, for the same problem (5), also defined in a convex smooth and bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, but with source term gg such that −c0​(s+sα)≤g⁡(s)≤a−b​sα-c_{0}(s+s^{\alpha})\leq g(s)\leq a-bs^{\alpha}, for s≥0s\geq 0, and with some α>1\alpha>1, a≥0a\geq 0 and χ,b,c0>0\chi,b,c_{0}>0, global existence of very weak solutions, as well their boundedness properties and long time behavior are discussed in [26], [27] and also [28]. Finally, for the sake of completeness, it is worth to precise that even though in the logistic source the term −μ​u2-\mu u^{2}, with μ>0\mu>0, corresponds to a death rate of the cells distribution and generally contrasts blow-up phenomena, in [31] is shown that under radially symmetric assumptions there exist initial data such that the corresponding solution of systems type (5) blows up (we also refer to [14] for techniques used to estimate the blow up time of unbounded solutions to system related to (5)).

To the best of our knowledge, deserving results in the direction of this present investigation which are tied to (2) under a perturbation for the evolution of uu through a logistic source, are the following. In a bounded and smooth domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, and under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, the system

(6) {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(uχ(v)∇v)+g(u)x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−u​f​(v)x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(u\chi(v)\nabla v)+g(u)&x\,\in\,\Omega,\,\,\,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uf(v)&x\,\in\,\Omega,\,\,\,t>0,\end{cases}
  1. i)

    for D⁡(u)=δ>0D(u)=\delta>0, χ⁡(v)=χ>0\chi(v)=\chi>0, g⁡(u)≤k​u−μ​uγg(u)\leq ku-\mu u^{\gamma}, with g⁡(0)≥0g(0)\geq 0, k≥0k\geq 0, μ>0\mu>0 and γ>1\gamma>1, and sufficiently regular initial data (u0,v0),(u_{0},v_{0}), admits for suitable small χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} a global and bounded classical solution (see [2]);

  2. ii)

    for D⁡(u)≡1D(u)\equiv 1, χ⁡(v)≤χ0(1+a​s)b\chi(v)\leq\frac{\chi_{0}}{(1+as)^{b}}, with χ0,a,b>0\chi_{0},a,b>0, g⁡(u)≤k​u−μ​u2g(u)\leq ku-\mu u^{2}, with g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and k,μ>0k,\mu>0, and sufficiently regular initial data (u0,v0,)(u_{0},v_{0},) admits for χ0​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)≤16​(n+1)\chi_{0}\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{1}{6(n+1)} a global and bounded classical solution (see [37]);

  3. iii)

    for D⁡(u)≡1D(u)\equiv 1, χ⁡(v)=χ>0\chi(v)=\chi>0, k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R}, g⁡(u)=k​u−μ​u2g(u)=ku-\mu u^{2}, and sufficiently regular initial data (u0,v0),(u_{0},v_{0}), admits for μ\mu larger compared to χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} a global and bounded classical solution and a weak one for arbitrary μ>0\mu>0 (see [12]).

Remark 1.

As shown in the corresponding proofs, we conclude this section observing that the contribution summarized in iii) explicitly provides conditions which connects v0v_{0} to the coefficient μ\mu of the logistic term gg; this does not hold for the items i) and ii). Nevertheless, the term χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} appears in these same works (as well in the mentioned assumption (4) of [21]), so that it seems a very proper quantity which coherently characterizes the nature of models type (6); consequently it will play a crucial role also in our main result.

2. Main result and structure of the paper

In agreement with all of the above, this paper is dedicated to the following problem

(7) {ut=∇⋅((u+1)m−1∇u−(u+1)αχ(v)∇v)+ku−μu2x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v​ux∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0​and​v​(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot((u+1)^{m-1}\nabla u-(u+1)^{\alpha}\chi(v)\nabla v)+ku-\mu u^{2}&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-vu&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0\,\,\textrm{and}\,\,\,v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0&x\in\Omega,\end{cases}

defined in a bounded and smooth domain Ω\Omega of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, where (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is a pair of nonnegative functions from (W1,r​(Ω))2,(W^{1,r}(\Omega))^{2}, for some r>max⁡{n,2}r>\max\{n,2\}, and m,k,μ∈ℝm,k,\mu\in\mathbb{R} with μ>0\mu>0. Moreover, we assume that

(8) α<m+12,\alpha<\frac{m+1}{2},

and that the function χ\chi generalizes the standard chemotactic sensitivity

(9) χ⁡(v)=χ0(1+a​v)2with some χ0>0anda≥0;\chi(v)=\frac{\chi_{0}}{(1+av)^{2}}\quad\textrm{with some }\quad\chi_{0}>0\quad\textrm{and}\quad a\geq 0;

exactly, χ∈C2​([0,∞))\chi\in C^{2}([0,\infty)) and satisfies for any v≥0v\geq 0 this growth condition

(10) χ⁡(v)≤χ0(1+a​v)bwith some χ0>0anda≥0andb>0.\chi(v)\leq\frac{\chi_{0}}{(1+av)^{b}}\quad\textrm{with some }\quad\chi_{0}>0\quad\textrm{and}\quad a\geq 0\quad\textrm{and}\quad b>0.

Specifically, the aim of the present article is to prove the existence of global and bounded classical solutions to (7) under some largeness assumption on μ\mu (whose value will depend on n,mn,m and α\alpha) with respect to some combination of powers of χ0​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi_{0}\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}, precisely in accordance to Remark 1 of the previous section.

Remark 2.

The problem studied in this paper generalizes some of the aforementioned examples. For instance, starting from the case in which no logistic source affects the system (i.e. k=μ=0k=\mu=0), in (7) the limit values m=α=1m=\alpha=1 and χ⁡(v)=χ>0\chi(v)=\chi>0 recover (2); further, in presence of logistic perturbations, the models discussed in items i), ii) and iii) are also easily deducible from (7) through evident choices of its data.

Additionally, we also observe that the first equation of (7) can be equivalent rewritten as

ut=∇⋅((u+1)m−1∇u−(u+1)α∇Θ(v))+ku−μu2x∈Ω,t>0,u_{t}=\nabla\cdot((u+1)^{m-1}\nabla u-(u+1)^{\alpha}\nabla\Theta(v))+ku-\mu u^{2}\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,

where in view of assumption (10) we have that Θ(v)=−∫v∞χ(s)ds\Theta(v)=-\int_{v}^{\infty}\chi(s)ds is finite. In this sense, it could be checked that the main result herein applies whenever Θ\Theta is smooth and nondecreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and satisfies

Θ⁡(s)=sβ1+a​sβa≥0,β>0ands≥0.\Theta(s)=\frac{s^{\beta}}{1+as^{\beta}}\quad a\geq 0,\,\beta>0\quad\textrm{and}\quad s\geq 0.

This last expression for Θ\Theta includes also the cases below, which are biologically coherent (see [16] and [17]),

Θ⁡(s)=s1+a​sandΘ⁡(s)=s21+a​s2ands≥0,\Theta(s)=\frac{s}{1+as}\quad\textrm{and}\quad\Theta(s)=\frac{s^{2}}{1+as^{2}}\quad\textrm{and}\quad s\geq 0,

the first one behaving actually as our prototype (9).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Once in §\lx@sectionsign3 some preparatory and well-known preliminaries are given, §\lx@sectionsign4 is focused on the derivation of a result concerning local-in-time existence of a classical solution (u,v)(u,v) to system (7) and on some crucial properties tied to the uu- and vv-components. Thereafter, in §\lx@sectionsign5, we define a sort of energy for such a local solution, which for some suitable p>1p>1 is defined as Φ⁡(t):=∫Ω(u+1)p+χ02​p​∫Ω|∇v|2​p\Phi(t):=\int_{\Omega}(u+1)^{p}+\chi_{0}^{2p}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2p}. In this way, by relying on general functional and algebraic relations, we establish that this energy satisfies a differential inequality, under a certain initial condition, whose right hand side is a power function which possesses a positive root. Subsequently, by means of a comparison principle, we provide a local-in-time independent bound for Φ⁡(t)\Phi(t), and hence in particular for uu in Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) and ∇v\nabla v in L2​p​(Ω)L^{2p}(\Omega). Finally, also in the same §\lx@sectionsign5, an application of a general and extensively used boundedness result for parabolic equations allows us to deduce from these gained estimates that the local classical solution is actually bounded and, then, also global. This represents exactly our main assertion:

Theorem 2.1.

Let Ω\Omega be a smooth and bounded domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, with n≥1n\geq 1. For given m,k∈ℝm,k\in\mathbb{R}, and μ\mu positive, let us assume that χ∈C2​([0,∞))\chi\in C^{2}([0,\infty)) satisfies relation (10) for some α\alpha as in (8). Then for any couple of nonnegative functions (u0,v0)∈(W1,r​(Ω))2(u_{0},v_{0})\in(W^{1,r}(\Omega))^{2}, with r>max⁡{n,2}r>\max\{n,2\}, it is possible to find two positive constants K1=K1​(n,m,α)K_{1}=K_{1}(n,m,\alpha) and K2=K2​(n,m,α)K_{2}=K_{2}(n,m,\alpha) such that if

(11) μ>K1​(n,m,α)​∥χ0​v0∥L∞​(Ω)2n+K2​(n,m,α)​∥χ0​v0∥L∞​(Ω)2​n,\mu>K_{1}(n,m,\alpha)\lVert\chi_{0}v_{0}\rVert^{\frac{2}{n}}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+K_{2}(n,m,\alpha)\lVert\chi_{0}v_{0}\rVert^{2n}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},

problem (7) admits a unique global classical solution (u,v)(u,v) which is uniformly bounded; more precisely, there exists a positive constant CC such that

(12) ∥u⁡(⋅,t)∥L∞​(Ω)+∥v⁡(⋅,t)∥W1,r​(Ω)≤Cfor allt∈(0,∞).\lVert u(\cdot,t)\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\lVert v(\cdot,t)\rVert_{W^{1,r}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\textrm{for all}\quad t\in(0,\infty).

3. Some preparatory tools

The following Lemmas are used through the paper to prove the main theorem. In particular, we mainly summarize some general functional inequalities, other proper technical results, and we close the section by adjusting some parameters which are necessary in our logical steps.

Lemma 3.1.

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded and smooth domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1,n\geq 1, and q≥1q\geq 1. For all f∈C2​(Ω)f\in C^{2}(\Omega), we have

(13) (Δ​f)2≤n​|D2​f|2,(\Delta f)^{2}\leq n|D^{2}f|^{2},
(14) |D2f∇f|2≤|D2f|2|∇f|2,\lvert D^{2}f\nabla f\rvert^{2}\leq|D^{2}f|^{2}\lvert\nabla f\rvert^{2},

and for all f∈C2​(Ω¯)f\in C^{2}(\bar{\Omega}) satisfying f​∂f∂ν=0f\frac{\partial f}{\partial\nu}=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega,

(15) ∥∇f∥L2​q+2​(Ω)2​q+2≤2​(4​q2+n)​∥f∥L∞​(Ω¯)2​∥|∇f|q−1​D2​f∥L2​(Ω)2,\lVert\nabla f\rVert^{2q+2}_{L^{2q+2}(\Omega)}\leq 2(4q^{2}+n)\lVert f\rVert^{2}_{L^{\infty}(\bar{\Omega})}\lVert|\nabla f|^{q-1}D^{2}f\rVert^{2}_{L^{2}(\Omega)},

where D2​fD^{2}f represents the Hessian matrix of ff and |D2f|2=∑i,j=1nfxi​xj2.|D^{2}f\rvert^{2}=\sum\limits_{i,j=1}^{n}f_{x_{i}x_{j}}^{2}.

Proof.

Straightforward calculations infer

(Δ​f)2=(∑i=1nfxi​xi)2=∑i,j=1nfxi​xi​fxj​xj≤∑i,j=1n(12​fxi​xi2+12​fxj​xj2)=n​∑i=1nfxi​xi2≤n​∑i,j=1nfxi​xj2=n​|D2​f|2,\begin{split}(\Delta f)^{2}=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{x_{i}x_{i}}\Big)^{2}&=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}f_{x_{i}x_{i}}f_{x_{j}x_{j}}\leq\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\Big(\frac{1}{2}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{i}}+\frac{1}{2}f^{2}_{x_{j}x_{j}}\Big)\\ &=n\sum_{i=1}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{i}}\leq n\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}=n\lvert D^{2}f\rvert^{2},\end{split}

and that

|D2f∇f|2=∑i,j=1nfxi​xj2​fxi2+∑i,j=1i≠jn2​fxi​xi​fxi​xj​fxi​fxj≤∑i,j=1nfxi​xj2​fxi2+∑i,j=1i≠jn(fxi​xi2​fxj2+fxi​xj2​fxi2)=∑i,j=1nfxi​xi2​fxj2+2​∑i,j=1i≠jnfxi​xj2​fxi2=|D2​f|2​|∇f|2.\begin{split}\lvert D^{2}f\nabla f\rvert^{2}&=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}f^{2}_{x_{i}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}2f_{x_{i}x_{i}}f_{x_{i}x_{j}}f_{x_{i}}f_{x_{j}}\\ &\leq\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}f^{2}_{x_{i}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}(f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{i}}f^{2}_{x_{j}}+f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}f^{2}_{x_{i}})\\ &=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{i}}f^{2}_{x_{j}}+2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}f^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}f^{2}_{x_{i}}=\lvert D^{2}f\rvert^{2}\lvert\nabla f\rvert^{2}.\end{split}

Relations (13) and (14) are so shown. As to (15), this is Lemma 2.2 of [12]. ∎

Remark 3.

As it can be observed, the hypothesis for the proofs of Theorems 14.4, 14.5 and 14.6 of [1] are more general that those fixed in our Lemma 4.1, so that it holds also under weaker restrictions on the data of problem (7).
